top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: The search strategy was developed in collaboration with an experienced research librarian. The search strategy consisted of MeSH terms including Point-of-Care Testing; Health Promotion; Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice; Patient Education as Topic; Health Literacy; Health Education; Life Style; Diet; Exercise; Health Behaviour; Smoking Cessation; Smoking Reduction; Tobacco Use Cessation; Alcohol Abstinence; Social Behaviour; and Social Participation. Keywords included domains of point-of-care (point of care, bedside, rapid, handheld, remote, mobile), testing (test, screening, diagnosis, monitor), patient (health, informed consent, disease, condition), knowledge (awareness, understanding, competence, comprehension), and behaviour (lifestyle, weight, diet, physical activity, alcohol, social, engage, community, smoking, tobacco). The term 'review' was excluded by title and manuscript type. No filters were applied. A full search strategy by database can be found in Additional file 2.

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: This study was strengthened by the rigorous systematic review process conducted in line with the PRISMA statement [17]. Eligibility criteria were explicitly defined prior to commencing the literature search, with no restrictions imposed on language, region, or study type. The search strategy was methodologically developed in collaboration with an experienced research librarian, following multiple pilot searches to refine database queries and MeSH terms across several databases to maximise coverage. Although comprehensive, the omission of device-specific and risk-factor terms may have limited retrieval of eligible studies, and citation searching was not undertaken. Future reviews should expand search terms to include specific NCDs, risk factors, and device-specific terminology to ensure broader coverage. Study screening and data extraction were independently undertaken by two researchers, achieving high agreement, which improves reliability compared to single screening methods [35]. Included studies were limited to publications from the five years prior to the search, an intentional scope decision aligned with WHO guidance to capture contemporary evidence for POC tests and health literacy definitions. As the final search was conducted in May 2023, the study is limited in its consideration of more recent evidence or developments in POC testing, and the findings should be interpreted as reflecting the evidence base up to that date. Although newer studies may now exist, findings remain highly relevant and provide a valuable foundation for understanding the role of modern POC testing in health literacy. Additionally, 11 full-text reports were unable to be retrieved, largely due to being abstract-only or presented in nonwritten formats. While these reports may lack sufficient methodological detail for full appraisal, their exclusion may still introduce retrieval bias and contribute to the narrow evidence base identified. Meta-analysis was not feasible due to variability between interventions, disease focus, measurement tools, and population characteristics. Outcomes were assessed using diverse instruments, ranging from validated tools (e.g. PAM-13) to study-developed questionnaires, qualitative interviews, and clinical markers of adherence or control. This mix of validated and self-reported proxy measures introduces differences in measurement rigour, further limiting comparability across studies. Despite this, shared self-reported proxy outcomes such as patient knowledge, confidence, engagement, and behaviour change enabled narrative synthesis via the framework of WHO health literacy actions. Designs were predominantly cross-sectional or short-term, with limited longitudinal follow-up. Furthermore, equity indicators were inconsistently reported, limiting disaggregated analysis. Although age and sex variables were consistently reported, ethnicity and socioeconomic indicators were often absent, restricting the ability to generalise findings to diverse populations. These limitations highlight the need for more consistent measurements using validated health literacy instruments, longer follow-ups, and systematic equity reporting in future work. While risk of bias assessment using the MMAT demonstrated generally strong methodological quality across the included studies, several limitations were also identified. Several studies did not adequately account for potential confounders, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of POC testing. Two studies did not meet the criterion for appropriate interpretation of results based on the data provided [27, 29], however this was addressed by considering only the raw outcome data in the synthesis. One study did not meet the criterion for low non-response bias [30], potentially affecting the representativeness of its findings. Although these issues were present in a minority of studies, they may reduce confidence in some reported associations and should be considered when interpreting the overall strength of the evidence base.

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Records were identified by a research librarian and researcher (KM) through searches of electronic databases from 5 May 2018 to the date of the search, 5 May 2023. Databases searched included Medline (via OVID), PsycINFO (via OVID), Emcare (via OVID), Scopus, ProQuest (Health and Medicine databases only), CINAHL (via EBSCO), and Web of Science (via Clarivate). Citation searches were not conducted.

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Resulting records from each database were imported into EndNote 20 where duplicates were provisionally removed. Records were then uploaded to Covidence systematic review management software [18] where a final duplication detection test was conducted. Titles and abstracts of resulting records were initially screened against eligibility criteria by two researchers (KM and LD), independently. Agreement between reviewers was high at 96.7%, with consensus required for further screening. Remaining records underwent independent full-text screening by the same two researchers (KM and LD), with consensus required for inclusion in the review. Agreement at full-text screening was 85.7%, with discrepancies resolved through discussion or, if necessary, adjudication by a third reviewer (MS).

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: The database searches resulted in the identification of 12,459 records (Fig. 1). After removing duplicates, 6,129 unique records were retained for screening (Fig. 1). Title and abstract screening resulted in 98 records for further screening. Of these, 11 reports could not be retrieved (abstract-only, n = 7; non-written format, n = 2; inaccessible, n = 2), leaving 87 articles retained for full-text screening (Fig. 1). Thirteen articles were eligible for inclusion following the final screening stage (Fig. 1). This reduction highlights the limited availability of recent evidence investigating POC testing and health literacy outcomes.
